sweep_summary: Three title hits for Dyirbal. (1) Pensalfini 2000 (ALS 1999 proceedings) was not previously held; the Glottolog UWA URL is dead but the ALS society's own proceedings archive serves the PDF openly (fetched sources, 15 pp., read in full). It restates Dixon 1972's pattern (initial, alternating, never final; primary/secondary ignored) and formalises the root|suffix footing break; it refines but does not change the catalog's fixed-strict coding and does not supersede Dixon 1972. (2) Maxwell 1981 (German, 10 pp., in the Münster 1980 Linguistisches Kolloquium Akten, Niemeyer) exists only as a De Gruyter paywalled chapter, DOI 10.1515/9783111355177.75; the De Gruyter, HathiTrust (search-only) and Google Books (no preview) routes were all blocked, so no text or abstract was read; priority medium (title is squarely about Dyirbal word accent, but it is a 1981 theoretical paper that almost certainly rests on Dixon's data). (3) Crowhurst 1995 WCCFL 13 is the published version of the ROA-19 preprint already held and read on 2026-09-16 (refines: morphology-sensitive secondary stress). No new first-hand descriptive statement was found; the deciding source remains Dixon 1972 §7.2 (held only as Google Books snippets, still the top acquisition wish). the Internet Archive was offline; discovery therefore went through the ALS site, Crossref, the HathiTrust volumes API and Google Books web pages. All fetches and receipts are under with.

new_statements.quote: The five languages can be characterised in the same way with respect to stress on monomorphemic words: stress falls on the first syllable and on every second syllable thereafter, but never on the final syllable || Dyirbal, illustrated in (3), allows a single foot to contain material from two suffixes, but never to contain one nucleus from the root and another from a suffix. This means that while a monosyllabic affix can be stressed if other affixes follow, a monomorphemic word with an odd number of syllables can never have its final syllable stressed.
new_statements.citation: Pensalfini, Rob (2000). Suffix coherence and stress in Australian languages. Proceedings of the 1999 Conference of the Australian Linguistic Society, pp. 1-3 (§2, §2.3).
new_statements.locator: p.1 §2 (general statement for Pintupi, Diyari, Dyirbal, Warlpiri, Jingulu) and pp.2-3 §2.3 'Dyirbal', ex.(3a-d); data attributed to Dixon 1972:274, 284 and Crowhurst 1994/Dixon p.c.
new_statements.reading: Initial stress with alternating secondary stress on odd non-final syllables in monomorphemic words (fixed-strict, matches the catalog's kind and rule string). In polymorphemic words the root keeps its own footing and suffix footing restarts at the root|suffix boundary, so a trisyllabic root plus suffixes gives 100(10)0-type patterns rather than strict 10100: the same morphology-sensitive refinement Crowhurst 1994 and Alderete 2009 already supplied. Pensalfini explicitly ignores the primary/secondary distinction. This is a secondary source whose Dyirbal data come entirely from Dixon 1972 (and Dixon p.c. via Crowhurst), so it does not replace Dixon 1972 §7.2 as the deciding source.

audit.action: cite a better source for the same coding
audit.recode_to: Keep kind fixed-strict (initial primary stress, exceptionless; final never stressed). Annotate the rule string: 10/100/1010/10100/101010... is Dixon's 'preferred'/mono-morphemic pattern; in polymorphemic words with a trisyllabic root secondary stress restarts at the root-affix boundary (σσσ+σσ → 10010, σσσ+σ+σσ → 100100; Dixon 1972:274-5 via Crowhurst 1994 ex.4, Alderete 2009 App.B), and Dixon 1972:275 reports no phonetic primary/secondary distinction.

sources.note: Secondary OT/metrical account (data from Dixon 1972, not new fieldwork). Monomorphemic words: initial stress, alternating on every second syllable, never final; primary/secondary distinction 'ignored'. Polymorphemic words: trochees restart at the root|suffix boundary (no foot straddles root and suffix), but a foot may span two suffixes: (wánydyi)-ngu, (wánydyi)-(ngú-gu), (dyángga)-(ná-mbi)la, (mánda)lay-m(bál-bi)la. Pensalfini's 'UNIEXPRT undominated' = roots keep the same stress pattern affixed or not.

sources.citation: Alderete, John. 2009. Exploring recursivity, stringency, and gradience in the Pama-Nyungan stress continuum. Ms./chapter, Rutgers RUcore doi:10.7282/t38c9t89 (data appendix B from Dixon 1972:274-275, 280, 284 and Dixon p.c.).
sources.quote: Mono-morphemic words: 'Main stress on the first syllable and alternating stress on every nonfinal odd syllable' (matches our rule string). Poly-morphemic: Dyirbal 'foot parsing restarts at the root|affix juncture' except /σσσ|σ/: (óo)(ó|o) búrguɽúm-bu (Alderete corrects Crowhurst's 1000 to 1010 per Dixon p.c.), /σσσ|σσ/ (óo)o|(óo) búrbula|gára = 10010, /σσσ|σ-σσ/ mándalay|mbál-bila = 100100, /σσ|σ-σσ/ d̢áŋga|ná-mbila = 10100. Also notes Dixon 1972:275 'no evidence that speakers ... phonetically distinguish two degrees of stress'.

sources.quote: Like Diyari, Dyirbal (i) avoids stress on a sole monosyllabic suffix after a disyllabic or trisyllabic root, (4a,b). In a sequence of monosyllabic suffixes, however, Dyirbal assigns stress to the first of each pair, proceeding from left to right, (4c,d,e,f). More striking is the fact that when a monosyllabic suffix is flanked by a root and a following disyllabic suffix, as in (4g,h), the monosyllable is stressed and the initial syllable of the following suffix is not.

sources.note: Secondary OT account of Dixon 1972's stress-marked forms: initial stress in every morpheme of 2+ syllables, quantity-insensitive disyllabic trochees, no monosyllabic feet (so never final stress: *(ëúgum)(bíl)); heteromorphemic footing allowed only when the foot's left edge is a morpheme's left edge, so the final syllable of a trisyllabic root is never footed with a following suffix: (búrgu)ɽum-bu, (bána)gay-(mbá-ri)-ɲu, (mánda)lay-(mbál-bi)la, but (búyba)-(rí-ɲu), (núdil)-(mál-ɖa)-ɲu.

sources.citation: Crowhurst, Megan J. 1994. Prosodic alignment and misalignment in Diyari, Dyirbal, & Gooniyandi: an optimizing approach. WCCFL 13; Rutgers Optimality Archive ROA-19 (10 pp).
sources.quote: Initial main stress, final syllable never stressed, no monosyllabic feet; but footing is morphology-sensitive: a sole monosyllabic suffix after a di/tri-syllabic root is unstressed and the final syllable of a trisyllabic root is never footed with a following suffix, so (búrgu)ɽum-bu 'jumping ant-ERG' = 1000, (bána)gay-(mbá-ri)-ɲu = 100100, (mánda)lay-(mbál-bi)la = 100100, while (búyba)-(rí-ɲu) = 1010 and (núdil)-(mál-da)-ɲu = 10100.
sources.locator: §1 ex.(4) and fn.3 (txt lines 82-136), §4 (lines 390-570); data cited to Dixon 1972:274,275,280,284 + Dixon p.c.
